companyCaseStudy.title: How Discord Scaled Real‑Time Chat to 140M+ Users: Sharding, BEAM, and a 10x Cost/Latency Win
companyCaseStudy.summary: Discord went from a handful of servers struggling with millions of persistent WebSocket connections to a highly sharded, BEAM‑powered real‑time gateway that supports 100s of millions of users and multi‑millions of concurrent users — cutting per‑message latency and reducing infrastructure cost by orders of magnitude.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook — a real‑time scaling headache

Imagine keeping open millions of WebSocket connections, delivering messages with <200ms end‑to‑end latency, and surviving huge, unpredictable spikes when a streamer goes live. Discord publicly reported ~140M+ monthly active users (MAU) around 2020 and multi‑millions of concurrent users in peaks. Their original stack started to creak under the scale: memory per connection, fan‑out costs, and so‑so reliability under hot shards.

This is the story of how Discord rebuilt its realtime layer — trading vertical scaling and brittle processes for a sharded, BEAM/Elixir‑style gateway, careful presence & fan‑out design, and data plane separation — and what measurable wins they saw.

---

## Problem: millions of long‑lived connections + high fan‑out

- Persistent connections are expensive: each WebSocket consumes memory and file descriptors. With millions of concurrent sockets, the per‑connection cost multiplied fast.
- Fan‑out is brutal: a message in a large community (guild) must be delivered to tens of thousands of members with minimal latency.
- Spiky load: gaming/streaming events produce sudden bursts — 10× traffic in a few seconds is common.
- The old approach (monolithic gateway processes, per‑message DB writes for presence) resulted in frequent hotspots and high ops overhead.

Requirements:
- Support millions of concurrent connections
- Sub‑200ms message propagation for normal cases
- Graceful handling of spikes and gradual cost growth

---

## Challenge: design constraints and tradeoffs

- Single machine cannot hold too many sockets reliably (memory limits, GC pauses). Language/runtime choice matters for many lightweight processes.
- Need for locality: delivering a message to 50k users should not cross every datacenter hop per recipient.
- Durable storage vs in‑memory presence: writing every presence update to the DB kills throughput.
- Avoid single points of failure: the gateway layer must be horizontally scalable and independently deployable.

---

## Solution: shard the gateway, move the concurrency to BEAM, separate concerns

High level decisions Discord made (public engineering signals + talks):
- Adopt a BEAM/Erlang/Elixir approach for the gateway layer to take advantage of millions of lightweight processes and predictable latency under concurrency.
- Shard connections by guild/region so that most message fan‑outs are local to a shard/process cluster.
- Use an in‑memory fast store (Redis/ETS) for presence and small TTLs rather than writing every event to a relational DB.
- Separate the ingestion (gateway) from durable storage (message history) — keep the real‑time path fast and minimal; persist async to Cassandra/Postgres for history/search.
- Implement efficient fan‑out workers and rate limiting at the dispatch layer so a hot message doesn't take down the gateway.

Mermaid architecture (simplified):

```mermaid
graph LR
  Client[Client (web/mobile)] --> LB[Edge Load Balancer]
  LB --> GatewayCluster((Gateway Shard Cluster))
  subgraph GatewayCluster
    GW1[Gateway Node 1]
    GW2[Gateway Node 2]
    GW3[Gateway Node N]
  end
  GatewayCluster -->|Publish events| Dispatch[Dispatch Layer (workers)]
  Dispatch --> Presence[Presence Store (Redis/ETS)]
  Dispatch --> FanoutWorkers[Local Fanout Workers]
  FanoutWorkers --> GatewayCluster
  Dispatch --> AsyncStore[(Durable Store — Cassandra/Postgres)]
  Client -->|Subscribe presence| Presence

  style GatewayCluster fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px
```

Key pieces explained:
- Edge LBs do TCP/TLS termination and route to gateway shards.
- Gateway nodes (BEAM/Elixir) own large numbers of sockets and run lightweight processes for each connection and channel subscription.
- Dispatch layer coordinates cross‑shard messages and triggers local fan‑out workers.
- Presence is stored in a fast volatile store: local ETS for node‑local fast lookups + Redis clusters for cross‑node queries (with TTLs and delta updates).
- Durable writes (message history, search indexing, audit) are handled asynchronously so the hot path stays low‑latency.

---

## Concrete tactics (engineering decisions)

1) Use BEAM (Elixir/Erlang) for the gateway
- BEAM gives millions of tiny processes, preemptive scheduling, and consistent latency under concurrency spikes.
- Result: fewer gateway machines required and lower tail latency vs heavy GC languages in similar roles.

2) Shard by guild / region
- Each gateway shard owns a subset of guilds and client subscriptions so most fan‑out is intra‑shard and local.
- When cross‑shard delivery is required, dispatch layer fanouts via optimized RPCs, not naive broadcast.

3) Presence: local ETS + Redis as a distributed cache
- Local ETS keeps node‑local subscriptions instant. Global presence uses Redis with short TTLs and delta publishing.
- Avoids constant DB writes and allows cheap presence reconciliation on reconnect.

4) Async durable path
- Keep the real‑time path in memory and non‑blocking. Persist messages to Cassandra/Postgres/Elastic asynchronously for history, search, and analytics.
- This avoids tail latencies during spikes.

5) Fanout workers & per‑guild rate limits
- Workers perform batched writes to sockets and enforce per‑guild/per‑user rate limiting to prevent hot messages from cascading failures.

---

## Results — measured wins (what changed)

| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------|-------|
| Typical E2E chat latency | ~200–500ms | ~50–150ms |
| Connections per gateway node | ~5k–10k (heavy memory) | ~50k–200k (BEAM lightweight processes) |
| Number of gateway servers | Hundreds | Tens (per region) |
| Operational incidents from gateway overload | Regular during spikes | Rare — graceful degradation via rate limits |
| Cost for real‑time tier | High (many machines) | ~3–10× lower (fewer nodes + better density) |

Notes on the numbers: these are synthesized from Discord engineering signals and public talks — the key point is order‑of‑magnitude reductions in both tail latency and server count after moving to a sharded, BEAM‑based approach with local presence.

---

## Visual flow: message send → fanout

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U[User sends message] --> G[Gateway node (owner of guild)]
  G --> D[Dispatch]
  D --> FW[Fanout worker]
  FW -->|Local subs| GWnodes[Gateway nodes (local shard)]
  FW -->|Cross‑shard| RPC[Dispatch RPC to other shards]
  RPC --> GWnodes
  GWnodes -->|Deliver ws| C[Clients]
  D --> Async[(Persist to history async)]
  Async --> DB[(Cassandra/Postgres)]
```

---

## Why this design worked (lessons)

- Put ephemeral, latency‑sensitive state in memory (presence, subscriptions) and persistent state in an async pipeline.
- Run the right runtime for the problem (BEAM for massive concurrency) — language/runtime tradeoffs matter.
- Shard by natural ownership (guild/region) to localize traffic and reduce cross‑network blasts.
- Enforce rate limits and backpressure close to the ingestion point to avoid cascading failures.

---

## Gotchas & operational notes

- BEAM is great for concurrency but you need to design for crash isolation and supervise processes correctly.
- Sharding moves complexity to the dispatch logic — make cross‑shard RPC efficient and observable.
- Presence consistency is eventually consistent; choose TTLs and reconciliation windows carefully for UX.
- Test spikes with realistic fan‑out patterns (guild message storms) — chaos testing pays.

---

## Epilogue — the business impact

By focusing on a specialized realtime plane (fast in‑memory presence + BEAM gateways + async persistence), Discord reduced tail latency, cut the number of gateway machines dramatically, and made their system resilient to the sudden audience explosions that come with high‑profile streams and events. The result: smoother UX for voice/text and a significantly lower ops footprint on the real‑time tier.
keyTakeaways: Use the right runtime: BEAM/Elixir is often a better fit for millions of lightweight long‑lived connections than heavy GCed languages.
Shard by ownership (guild/region) to localize fan‑out and reduce cross‑network cost; combine local in‑memory presence with a small distributed cache for global lookups.
Keep the hot path minimal: deliver messages from memory and persist asynchronously; add fan‑out workers and rate limits to protect the cluster during spikes.
companyCaseStudy.codeExample:
defmodule Gateway do
  use GenServer

  # simplified: track subscriptions in ETS and broadcast via PubSub
  def start_link(_), do: GenServer.start_link(__MODULE__, %{}, name: __MODULE__)

  def init(_) do
    :ets.new(:subs, [:named_table, :public, read_concurrency: true])
    {:ok, %{} }
  end

  def subscribe(user, channel) do
    :ets.insert(:subs, {channel, user})
  end

  def broadcast(channel, payload) do
    # read subscribers from ETS and send (batched)
    subs = :ets.lookup(:subs, channel)
    subs
    |> Enum.chunk_every(100) # batch sends to avoid flood
    |> Enum.each(fn batch ->
      Enum.each(batch, fn {_ch, user} ->
        send_ws(user, payload)
      end)
    end)
  end

  defp send_ws(user, payload) do
    # simplified: look up socket process and push
    case Registry.lookup(:sockets, user) do
      [{pid, _}] -> send(pid, {:push, payload})
      _ -> :ok
    end
  end
end

concept.title: Seeing the Invisible: Distributed Tracing & Observability Patterns
concept.summary: Distributed tracing makes the invisible interactions across microservices visible so you can find latency hotspots, failures, and weird behavior across services. It turns vague "it’s slow" incidents into actionable breadcrumbs that point to the exact service, span, and code path causing trouble.
concept.explanation:
## Why this matters — the real-world problem it solves

When your system is a single monolith, a slow request has a small number of places to look. In a microservices world a single user action can fan out to a dozen services, caches, queues, and databases. Without context you get fragments: logs in one service, a metric spike in another, and customer complaints. Distributed tracing threads the needle: it attaches a trace id to a request and records *spans* for each operation, letting you reconstruct the full timeline.

**Analogy:** imagine trying to debug why a package didn’t arrive by asking each postal worker for their memory of where it went. Tracing is like giving that package a GPS tracker — you can replay the journey and see the exact handoffs.

---

## How distributed tracing works (high level)

1. **Instrumentation:** code creates spans for logical operations (HTTP request, DB call, cache hit). Libraries or frameworks can auto-instrument common operations.
2. **Context propagation:** the trace id and span id are propagated across service boundaries (HTTP headers, message attributes). That keeps all spans part of the same trace.
3. **Sampling:** not every request needs to be stored. Sampling decides which traces to keep.
4. **Export & storage:** collected spans are exported to a collector/ingest service (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo) and stored for querying/visualization.
5. **UI & analysis:** trace timeline shows spans, durations, tags, logs, and errors — you can slice by latency, endpoint, or error.

### Visual: request flow with tracing
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant G as API_Gateway
  participant A as Service_A
  participant B as Service_B
  participant DB as Database
  participant TC as Trace_Collector

  C->>G: POST /checkout (trace-id)
  G->>A: POST /orders (ctx carries trace-id)
  A->>B: POST /payments (span: charge-card)
  B->>DB: SELECT / INSERT (span: write-payment)
  B-->>A: 200 OK (span end)
  A-->>G: 201 Created (span end)
  G-->>C: 201 Created (span end)
  G->>TC: Export spans
```

---

## Before / After (what you get)

| Before Distributed Tracing | After Distributed Tracing |
|---|---|
| "A payment failed sometime this morning" — no idea where | Trace shows Service_B returned 5xx on span "charge-card" at 10:12:03, with stack and payload
| Metrics show latency spike but not source | Timeline shows a slow DB call inside Service_B that explains the tail latency
| Correlating logs across services is manual and error-prone | Trace id links logs and spans across services for one request

---

## Traces vs Metrics vs Logs — quick comparison

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Traces | Show end-to-end request flow and causality; root-cause latency | Higher cardinality; storage cost | Troubleshooting latency, error paths across services
| Metrics | Lightweight, great for alerting and trends | Aggregated; lose per-request causality | Dashboards, SLOs, alerts
| Logs | Detailed, free-form context | Hard to correlate across services without trace id | Deep diagnostics for a specific service or span

---

## Practical example: instrumenting Node/Express (OpenTelemetry)

This minimal example shows auto-instrumentation, context propagation, and exporting to a collector (Jaeger).

```javascript
// install: @opentelemetry/sdk-node @opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node @opentelemetry/exporter-jaeger
const { NodeSDK } = require('@opentelemetry/sdk-node');
const { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } = require('@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node');
const { JaegerExporter } = require('@opentelemetry/exporter-jaeger');

const exporter = new JaegerExporter({ serviceName: 'orders-service' });
const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  traceExporter: exporter,
  instrumentations: [getNodeAutoInstrumentations()],
});

sdk.start();

// Now run an Express app. HTTP requests, DB clients, and common libraries are auto-instrumented.
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.post('/checkout', async (req, res) => {
  // You can create manual spans too
  const tracer = require('@opentelemetry/api').trace.getTracer('custom');
  const span = tracer.startSpan('process-checkout');
  try {
    // call downstream services, DB, etc.
    res.status(201).send('ok');
  } finally {
    span.end();
  }
});

app.listen(8080);
```

Note: in a polyglot system instrument each language and ensure HTTP/messaging headers propagate the trace context (W3C traceparent is the standard).

---

## When to use distributed tracing

- Microservices with cross-service latency or error causality.
- Systems with high tail latency where slow requests are caused by a particular downstream.
- Investigating production incidents that cause partial failures across components.

Not necessary for single small services or purely batch jobs where metrics and logs suffice.

---

## Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

- *No context propagation:* forget to propagate trace headers across async boundaries — you get fragmented traces. Use libraries that handle it or instrument the messaging layer.
- *Over-sampling or under-sampling:* storing everything is costly; sampling too aggressively hides rare errors. Use adaptive sampling for noisy endpoints, keep 100% of errors.
- *High-cardinality tags:* indexing user_id or raw UUIDs on every span increases storage and slows queries. Use low-cardinality service/route tags and keep sensitive/high-cardinality fields in logs rather than indexed tags.
- *PII in traces:* traces can carry payloads — ensure sensitive data is scrubbed or redacted before export.
- *Assuming traces alone answer everything:* correlate traces with metrics and logs. Traces point you to the hot span; logs give the payload and stack traces; metrics tell you if this is a trend.

---

## Rollout checklist (practical)

- Instrument one service end-to-end first (HTTP server, outgoing HTTP clients, DB). Verify spans appear in the UI.
- Ensure trace context is propagated through HTTP headers and message brokers.
- Configure sampling: keep all errors, sample tail and representative successful requests.
- Standardize semantic attributes (service.name, http.method, http.route, error=false/true).
- Add trace ids to logs to correlate (e.g., add trace_id in structured logs).
- Train on common queries: heatmaps, slow endpoints, the service map.

---

Distributed tracing doesn’t replace good metrics or logs — it completes them. When implemented correctly it turns production mysteries into a timeline you can inspect, filter, and act on.
keyTakeaways: Distributed tracing provides end-to-end visibility across microservices by recording causal spans and propagating trace context.
Instrument, propagate context, sample wisely, and avoid high-cardinality tags or leaking PII.
Use traces alongside metrics and logs: traces find the path, metrics detect the anomaly, logs give details.
